claim_text: It's fine when you eat it [fructose] with fruit because of the fiber that's associated with it
notes: BMJ umbrella review attributes the harms to free and added sugars and sugar-sweetened beverages, not to whole fruit.

claim_text: It drives dopamine receptors down and is highly addictive
notes: Only a narrative review and a rat reward study were retrieved. Nothing measures dopamine receptor downregulation or addiction in people, so this is insufficient evidence rather than support.

claim_text: It does not satiate you the same way that normal table sugar does, keeps you hungry compared to regular sugar
notes: The closest retrieved trial compares sucrose with glucose, not crystalline fructose with table sugar, so it does not test this comparison.

claim_text: [Fructose] produces more body fat
notes: Split from a compound sentence that also claimed physical inactivity. Umbrella review finds increased body weight and ectopic fat for sugar-sweetened beverages.

claim_text: [Fructose] produces ... physical inactivity. In other words, it makes you more sedentary
notes: Other half of the split compound claim. The video displays its source on screen and OCR recovered it: a 2015 Scientific Reports study in rodents, fructose against an isocaloric glucose diet. It does report decreased physical activity, but in animals, so directness fails for a claim stated about people.

claim_text: [Fructose] inhibits three enzymes critical for mitochondrial function, AMP kinase, ACADL, and CPT1
notes: A targeted search for fructose with AMPK/CPT1 and mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation returned nothing that tests this; the empty search is in evidence_cache/.

claim_text: It's also been shown to contribute to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
notes: Well supported, including a mechanistic Nature paper and two reviews in hepatology/nutrition.

claim_text: When fructose is absorbed without fiber, it causes the tight junctions in the epithelial cells ... to start to separate and there is some permeability
notes: Only a mechanistic overview of dietary carbohydrates in leaky-gut pathogenesis was retrieved. No human study tests fructose-without-fibre against intestinal permeability.

claim_text: It [high fructose corn syrup] contributes to cancer
notes: Downgraded from SUPPORTED after reading the source the video puts on screen. OCR recovered it as the 2015 review The role of fructose in metabolism and cancer, and the displayed page states that how dietary fructose impacts human cancer progression and the response to immunotherapy remains unresolved; the tumour data shown is in mice. The umbrella review's cancer associations are for dietary sugar broadly, not HFCS. Nothing retrieved tests this claim directly in people.

claim_text: It can contribute to metabolic disorders ... even without obesity being present
notes: Fructose-driven hepatic insulin resistance is documented independently of obesity.

claim_text: It's been shown to contribute to diabetes
notes: The 2025 dose-response meta-analysis finds the incident-T2D association for sugar consumed as beverages, and explicitly does not support it for total sugar or sucrose regardless of form. HFCS is predominantly consumed in beverages, so the claim holds in the form that matters, with that qualification.

claim_text: it puts you at greater risk for heart disease
notes: Umbrella review detects harmful associations with ten cardiovascular outcomes.

claim_text: A 2023 study showed that red 40 causes DNA damage
notes: Genuine conflict: a 2015 in vivo genotoxicity study of Allura Red AC reports genotoxicity, and a 2017 OECD-guideline study run in response to EFSA reports none. The 2017 study is industry-authored (IACM / Coca-Cola / Colorcon), which a reviewer should weigh. The speaker's 2023 study is real and OCR recovered it from the screen: Toxicology Reports 2023, PMID 37719200 -- but its own title ends in mice, so the species limitation applies to the supporting side too.

claim_text: [red 40 causes] colonic inflammation and affects the gut microbiome
notes: Both retrieved studies are in mice, including the one the video displays, whose title ends in mice. The Nature Communications study showing Allura Red AC promotes colitis susceptibility via intestinal serotonin is in mice. Directness fails for a claim stated about people.

claim_text: A 2022 study showed that synthetic food dyes are linked to ADHD in children
notes: The best-evidenced claim in the video. OCR recovered the on-screen citation and it is a 2022 systematic review of the human and animal evidence, so the speaker's date is right here. Three randomised placebo-controlled challenge trials back it independently. One qualification for the reviewer: those trials measure hyperactive behaviour in the general child population, not a diagnosis of ADHD.

claim_text: a 2015 study showed that it [synthetic food dyes] is linked directly to cancer
notes: OCR recovered the speaker's 2015 study from the screen: Anticancer Research 2015, DNA repair in human lymphocytes exposed to tartrazine yellow. It is an in vitro assay, it measures DNA repair rather than cancer, and it concerns tartrazine (yellow 5) rather than the red 40 the segment is built around, so it does not support linked directly to cancer. Per section 7 that makes it insufficient, not contradicted.

claim_text: A 2022 study showed that nitrates show an increased risk of cancer when ingested
notes: Matches the cited year: the 2022 NutriNet-Sante analysis finds higher breast cancer risk for food additive nitrates and higher prostate cancer risk for additive nitrites, with no association for natural sources -- a distinction the video does not make.

claim_text: [Agave syrup] is very high in fructose, usually about 57 to 90% fructose
notes: Settled from a section 6 reference (food composition), where PubMed searches had returned nothing. USDA FoodData Central's agave syrup record gives 55.6 g fructose and 12.43 g glucose per 100 g: fructose is about 56% of the syrup by weight and about 82% of its sugars, inside or at the edge of the claimed 57-90% on either reading. Medium confidence because one database entry stands for a product that varies by brand.

claim_text: you need to drink eight cups of water a day
notes: Searches for the eight-glasses rule and for adult water requirements returned nothing that tests it. The rule having no evidence base is exactly why it is a myth, but section 7 is explicit that absence of evidence is not contradiction, so the verdict is insufficient rather than CONTRADICTED. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled. Public-health fluid guidance is about total fluid as an aim, not a need for eight cups of water, so even where it exists it fails directness and the verdict stands.

claim_text: we only use 10% of our brain
notes: The neuromyths literature (PMID 23087664, 36470620) was retrieved, but neither abstract names the ten-percent claim, so citing them for it would be citing a paper for something not shown to be in it -- the evidence-laundering failure in section 7's probe. Left uncited rather than loosely cited. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): NCBI Bookshelf (StatPearls) is the right section 6 source, but Bookshelf pages answer scripted retrieval with a reCAPTCHA, so nothing could be read and the verdict stands.

claim_text: if you crack your knuckles you're going to get arthritis
notes: Directly tested and directly refuted: the case-control study concludes that a history of habitual knuckle cracking, including total duration and cumulative exposure, does not seem to be a risk factor for hand osteoarthritis. The one claim in this video the evidence can actually settle, and the one that makes the section 9 rules return DEBUNKING.

claim_text: to pee on a jellyfish sting and that that'll make it heal
notes: The 2025 systematic review of jellyfish-sting first aid lists the treatments with any evidence (seawater, heat, cold packs, lidocaine, vinegar, bicarbonate) and urine is not among them -- it is not tested at all, and the review rates the whole evidence base very low quality. Not tested is insufficient, not contradicted.

claim_text: if you shave your hair it'll grow back thicker
notes: Lynfield and MacWilliams, 'Shaving and hair growth' (J Invest Dermatol 1970), is exactly on the question, but PubMed holds no abstract for it and it is not in PMC, so its conclusion could not be read. Cited as the on-point paper; a reviewer with journal access should read it and will most likely upgrade this row to CONTRADICTED. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): NCBI Bookshelf (StatPearls) is the right section 6 source, but Bookshelf pages answer scripted retrieval with a reCAPTCHA, so nothing could be read and the verdict stands.

claim_text: people who eat a lot of saturated fats, which are totally fine, by the way
notes: Good studies point in different directions. The 2020 Cochrane review finds reducing saturated fat cuts combined cardiovascular events by 21% (moderate quality) though with little or no effect on all-cause or cardiovascular mortality; a 2025 meta-analysis of nine trials finds no significant difference in any of those outcomes and concludes that saturated fat reduction cannot currently be recommended. Exactly the case MIXED exists for.

claim_text: they replace some fraction of those [saturated fats] with seed oils. And in almost every study, the people are months later healthier
notes: The Cochrane review supports replacement with polyunsaturated fat reducing cardiovascular events, and the linoleic-acid meta-analysis points the same way; the 2025 meta-analysis finds no benefit. 'Almost every study' overstates a split literature, which is why this is MIXED rather than SUPPORTED.

claim_text: seed oils are super great for your health. They're totally fine
notes: The systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts concludes that dietary linoleic acid intake is inversely associated with coronary heart disease risk in a dose-response manner. Observational, and 'super great' is stronger than 'not harmful', hence medium confidence.

claim_text: you need to eliminate your sugar addiction. If you didn't know, your body runs off sugar, aka glucose. So if you stop feeding yourself sugar, your body will burn the sugar that is stored
notes: Roughly describes glycogen depletion, which is textbook physiology, but no retrieved study tests the claim as stated and 'sugar addiction' is not defined here. Honest insufficient rather than a verdict propped up by background knowledge.

claim_text: you need to be drinking a hundred ounces of water a day. Really, you should be drinking your body weight in ounces
notes: Same evidence gap as the eight-cups myth in v07, from the opposite stance: nothing retrieved establishes a body-weight-in-ounces water requirement. Note that v07 refutes a hydration rule and this video endorses a stricter one -- a useful pair for the stance step.

claim_text: your body actually flushes out the fat cells through your bloodstream, and you pee it out. You don't poop it out ... you pee out the fat
notes: THE ROW MOST LIKELY TO CHANGE ON REVIEW. Meerman and Brown, 'When somebody loses weight, where does the fat go?' (BMJ 2014), is precisely on this question, but PubMed carries only the teaser line 'explain why the answer might not be what you expect' and the paper has no PMCID, so nothing readable was retrieved. Three further searches for the mass balance of fat loss returned nothing usable. A reviewer who reads the full text should upgrade this to CONTRADICTED, which flips the video to MISINFO. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): NCBI Bookshelf (StatPearls) is the right section 6 source, but Bookshelf pages answer scripted retrieval with a reCAPTCHA, so nothing could be read and the verdict stands. The BMJ paper itself is not on the allow-list.

claim_text: don't worry about being hungry. I promise you that feeling goes away. You will stop being hungry after a while. Probably like a week probably like two weeks
notes: Nothing retrieved tests whether hunger resolves within one to two weeks of energy restriction. The adaptive-thermogenesis paper that the search returned measures resting energy expenditure, not appetite, so it does not test this.

claim_text: nine times out of ten you can't ... weigh 130 pounds and be eating pizzas and burgers
notes: No population, no quantity and no time frame: there is no version of this that a study could test as stated. Section 7's NOT_VERIFIABLE rather than INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, because the problem is the claim, not the literature.

claim_text: if I go out and I eat something real dirty for me ... I'm going to drink a lot of water, I'm gonna flush it out
notes: The idea that drinking water flushes out food already eaten. No retrieved study tests it.

claim_text: all of these foods behind me literally contain hundreds of dangerous chemicals
notes: Which foods, which chemicals, dangerous at what dose, for what outcome -- none are specified, and 'chemicals' covers water and salt as readily as anything else. There is no study that could test this as stated, so NOT_VERIFIABLE rather than INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE.

claim_text: How to know if you have ADHD: ... Very indecisive
notes: The list's framing sentence is carried on this row. Each item is a separate diagnostic assertion, so the list is split per section 4 rather than kept as one compound claim; they share a verdict and evidence. Contradicted by the content analysis of TikTok #adhdtest videos, which found 46 of 50 (92%) misleading, by the study of diagnostic risk in ADHD social-media content, and by the European Consensus Statement, under which adult ADHD requires clinical assessment of persistent, cross-situational, impairing symptoms with childhood onset -- not a checklist of common experiences.

claim_text: How to know if you have ADHD: ... Forgetting why you walked in a r[oo]m
notes: Nonspecific everyday experience presented as an ADHD indicator. Same evidence and reasoning as c1.

claim_text: How to know if you have ADHD: ... Reading a whole page and nothing goes in[,] so [you] have to read again
notes: Nonspecific everyday experience presented as an ADHD indicator. Same evidence and reasoning as c1.

claim_text: How to know if you have ADHD: ... Random bursts of energy
notes: Nonspecific everyday experience presented as an ADHD indicator. Same evidence and reasoning as c1.

claim_text: How to know if you have ADHD: ... Not sitting still until someone calls it [o]ut
notes: Nonspecific everyday experience presented as an ADHD indicator. Same evidence and reasoning as c1.

claim_text: How to know if you have ADHD: ... Mood swings
notes: Nonspecific everyday experience presented as an ADHD indicator. Same evidence and reasoning as c1.

claim_text: seed oils are horrible for you
notes: The myth the video exists to refute, stated in its opening line. The systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts finds dietary linoleic acid inversely associated with coronary heart disease risk in a dose-response manner, which contradicts 'horrible for you'. Observational evidence, hence medium confidence.

claim_text: In every single human study done, the people eating more seed oils either saw the same or actually better health outcomes than the groups eating less
notes: Unusually, the hedge inside the claim ('the same or better') is what makes it hold: the Cochrane review finds benefit from replacing saturated fat and the 2025 meta-analysis finds no difference, and both fall inside 'same or better'. 'Every single human study done' is an absolute that cannot be verified exhaustively, which is why this is medium confidence rather than high.

claim_text: researchers locked people in a metabolic ward and fed them two diets matched for the calories in sugar, fat, fiber, and sodium ... On the processed diet, people ate 500 calories more a day and gained weight
notes: An accurate description of a real trial, down to the effect size: Hall et al., 'Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake and Weight Gain: An Inpatient Randomized Controlled Trial of Ad Libitum Food Intake'. The most precisely sourced claim in the bundle that the speaker did not show on screen.

claim_text: Since the 1960s, Japan has quadrupled its vegetable oil intake in the form of canola and soybean ... Their obesity rate is under 5%, and they live longer than almost anyone on the earth
notes: Three national statistics (oil intake, obesity prevalence, life expectancy). All are checkable, but against OECD or WHO country data rather than the biomedical literature, and nothing retrievable through PubMed or a WHO/CDC page tests them. A structural gap in the evidence sources rather than a weakness in the claim -- see the PR description.

claim_text: We eat about 500 or more calories a day than we did in 1970
notes: Same kind of claim as the Japan one: a national food-availability statistic, not a biomedical finding.

claim_text: a remedy capable of relieving dry cough
notes: No trial of this preparation. The honey the video offers as an optional sweetener does have Cochrane evidence for acute cough in children, but that tests honey, not this decoction, so it is not cited here.

claim_text: a remedy capable of ... [relieving] bronchitis
notes: Searches for herbal treatment of acute bronchitis return trials of Pelargonium sidoides extract, a different preparation entirely, so nothing tests this claim.

claim_text: a remedy capable of ... expelling mucus stuck in the lungs
notes: A search for ginger as a respiratory expectorant returned nothing at all; the empty search is in evidence_cache/.

claim_text: a remedy capable of ... improving sinusitis
notes: Nothing retrieved tests any of these ingredients against sinusitis.

claim_text: a remedy capable of ... easing cold symptoms
notes: The closest direct test available: the Cochrane review of garlic for the common cold concludes there is insufficient clinical trial evidence for garlic in preventing or treating colds, resting on a single trial. Cited as the nearest evidence while the verdict stays insufficient, because the review itself reports an absence of evidence rather than a demonstrated lack of effect.

claim_text: You'll reduce abdominal fat. Studies show that almonds can help you lose weight, especially in the stomach area
notes: A meta-analysis of 37 randomised trials finds significant reductions in body weight (-0.45 kg) and waist circumference (-0.66 cm) with moderate GRADE certainty. Two caveats a reviewer should weigh: the effects are small, and the 'especially in the stomach area' part is not established -- certainty for visceral adipose tissue specifically was rated very low.

claim_text: Almonds are rich in unsaturated fats that promote good cholesterol and protect your heart
notes: No cardiovascular-outcome trial of almonds was retrieved, and the systematic review of nuts in secondary cardiovascular prevention found no change in lipid or inflammatory profiles. Not enough to call the claim false, well short of supporting it.

claim_text: Thanks to their fiber and protein content, almonds make you feel full. This makes them an ideal snack for controlling your appetite
notes: Individual trials point this way (almonds improve appetite-regulating hormones; snacking on almonds lowers energy intake against a high-carbohydrate snack), but the 37-trial meta-analysis rates the certainty of the appetite evidence very low on GRADE. Section 7's 'what exists is too weak' applies.

claim_text: Almonds are an excellent source of magnesium, which plays an essential role in mood regulation and stress management
notes: Every trial the search returned tests magnesium inside a multi-ingredient supplement (with B vitamins, green tea, rhodiola), so none isolates magnesium's effect on mood or stress.

claim_text: Almonds are naturally rich in tryptophan, an amino acid that plays a key role in the production of serotonin, the sleep hormone
notes: Nothing retrieved tests almond tryptophan against sleep in people -- the only hit was a study in ring doves. Worth a reviewer's attention separately: calling serotonin 'the sleep hormone' is wrong (melatonin is the one usually meant), but that is a mislabel inside the reasoning rather than a separate testable claim, and no retrieved source states it, so it is noted rather than cited.

claim_text: Almonds are rich in antioxidants like vitamin E, which help fight oxidative stress and reduce daily stress
notes: Conflates oxidative stress with psychological stress. Nothing retrieved tests vitamin E or almonds against perceived daily stress.

claim_text: You're going to be consuming the best quality protein. Your muscles, your connective tissue will get the highest quality amino acids
notes: A search for egg protein quality scores (DIAAS, biological value) returned nothing. Egg protein scoring well is uncontroversial nutrition-textbook material, but PubMed returned no source for it and section 7 does not allow filling the gap from background knowledge. A reviewer with a food composition reference should expect to upgrade this.

claim_text: Eggs are high in antioxidants, which is really good to prevent something called macular degeneration as well as cataracts
notes: The retrieved review covers lutein and zeaxanthin in age-related macular degeneration, not egg intake as a prevention strategy, and says nothing retrievable about cataracts. Indirect on both halves of the claim.

claim_text: Eggs are also high in something called choline, which is really good to prevent a fatty liver
notes: The Framingham analysis finds dietary choline intake strongly inversely associated with incident NAFLD risk, which is the claim as stated. But the same cohort found no association between egg intake itself and NAFLD risk, so the nutrient link holds while the food-level effect does not. A reviewer could reasonably call this MIXED; recorded as SUPPORTED because the sentence is a claim about choline.

claim_text: [choline is] really good to ... support your brain, better focus, concentration, and memory
notes: Split from the fatty-liver claim in the same sentence. Nothing retrieved tests choline or eggs against focus, concentration or memory.

claim_text: Even though eggs are high in cholesterol, you're going to find that your HDL, the good cholesterol will go up if you consume eggs
notes: Directly supported: the meta-analysis of randomised trials concludes that egg consumption increases total cholesterol, LDL-C and HDL-C against low-egg control diets. Supported exactly as stated -- and worth a reviewer's note that the same result includes the LDL rise the video leaves out, so a true claim is being used to carry a one-sided impression.

claim_text: if you eat eggs for breakfast, you're going to find your blood sugars are going to be very stabilized
notes: A search for egg breakfasts and postprandial glycaemia returned nothing; the nearest trial compares two eggs a day with an oatmeal breakfast and reports carotenoids and choline, not glucose stability.

claim_text: [vaccines] can cause everything from osteoporosis to autism
notes: Played as a clip and rejected by the framing that follows. The evidence-based meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies is titled 'Vaccines are not associated with autism'. The osteoporosis half of the claim is not separately tested by anything retrieved, but the autism half is squarely contradicted.

claim_text: The COVID vaccine introduction has had a catastrophic negative effect
notes: The global estimate finds more than 2.5 million deaths averted by COVID-19 vaccination over 2020-2024 (one death averted per 5400 doses), with sensitivity analyses between 1.4 and 4.0 million lives saved. A net catastrophic negative effect is the opposite of that.

claim_text: you can reverse autism through diet
notes: The systematic review of six randomised trials (214 participants) of gluten- and casein-free diets finds no statistically significant differences in autism core symptoms between groups, with one exception on a single communication subdomain. That refutes reversal through diet; medium confidence because the trials test one dietary approach rather than every possible one.

claim_text: [Cheerios carry harmful] glyphosate residues ... your cereal is a spawn of Satan
notes: The myth being refuted. Evidence genuinely points both ways on glyphosate and cancer, so MIXED. Note that the columns read against the claim, not against the speaker: papers supporting glyphosate harm sit in evidence_supporting because the claim asserts harm.

claim_text: when research actually studied this further and looked at glyphosate independently, it wasn't significantly associated with cancer at any site in a study of 54,000 people
notes: An accurate description of a real study, down to the cohort size: among 54,251 applicators, glyphosate was not statistically significantly associated with cancer at any site in unlagged analyses. What he leaves out, and a reviewer should see, is the same paper's finding of increased acute myeloid leukaemia risk in the highest exposure quartile (RR 2.44).

claim_text: a look at 15 government agencies and their consensus on glyphosate. Not genotoxic, doesn't represent a risk of cancer, not carcinogenic, not neurotoxic
notes: 'Consensus' overstates the position. The retrieved literature is explicitly about the disagreement between IARC, which classified glyphosate as a probable human carcinogen, and the regulatory agencies that did not. Papers exist arguing each way, which is MIXED, not consensus.

claim_text: an 150 pound adult would have to eat over 5,000 cups a day for a prolonged period of time for glyphosate to become an issue
notes: A dose calculation against EPA tolerance levels. Checkable in principle, but against a regulatory tolerance document rather than the biomedical literature, and nothing retrievable through PubMed or a WHO/CDC page tests it.

claim_text: High fructose corn syrup, our body doesn't really know what to do with it, it doesn't have the proper enzymes or stuff to break it down
notes: Quoted from the news clip and then refuted. Human fructose metabolism via intestinal and hepatic fructolysis is characterised in the retrieved review, so the enzymes plainly exist. The review describes the pathway rather than setting out to rebut this claim, hence medium confidence.

claim_text: by adding cane sugar instead of high fructose corn syrup, it wouldn't be as overwhelming to the liver and wouldn't have as high of blood sugar spikes
notes: Directly tested and directly refuted: in patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes, plasma glucose responses after sucrose and HFCS test meals 'did not differ', and the integrated areas under the glucose curves were not statistically different. Swapping one for the other does not reduce the spike.

claim_text: a beverage that is basically liquid sugar substituting one type of sugar for a very similar type of sugar is probably not gonna do a whole lot in the realm of making people healthier
notes: The speaker's own positive claim, supported by the same trial that refutes the clip. Appropriately hedged ('probably not gonna do a whole lot'), and the evidence is a small 1985 study in a diabetic population, so medium confidence.

claim_text: Since your glycogen stores are depleted overnight, your body switches to burning fat more quickly
notes: Higher fat oxidation during fasted exercise is the well-described part of this topic. Cited to the fed-versus-fasted interval training trial; note it is fat oxidation during exercise, which is not the same as losing more fat.

claim_text: your metabolism gets activated, helping you burn fat more efficiently, which makes weight loss easier and faster
notes: This is the step the video takes without support: greater fat oxidation during a fasted walk does not make weight loss faster. The trial that compares fed with fasted training found body-composition improvements in both states. Not a clean contradiction of the claim as worded, so insufficient, but this is the row a reviewer should look at first in this video.

claim_text: Your cortisol level, the stress hormone, gets regulated. This helps you feel more relaxed and calm throughout the day
notes: 'Regulated' is not a direction, and nothing retrieved tests morning fasted walking against cortisol or self-reported calmness.

claim_text: After just one week, your circulation improves. This helps regulate blood pressure and strengthens your cardiovascular system
notes: The systematic review concludes brisk walking significantly reduces blood pressure in people with hypertension. Two qualifications: the evidence is in hypertensive populations rather than everyone, and nothing establishes the 'after just one week' timeline the video asserts.

claim_text: After 20 days, your immune system becomes stronger
notes: The exercise-immunology literature that the search returned concerns infection susceptibility in athletes and training loads; none of it tests a 20-day immune effect from a daily 20-minute walk. The precise-sounding timeline has no source.

claim_text: Your sleep also improves. You fall asleep faster and wake up feeling more refreshed
notes: The meta-analysis of randomised trials finds exercise improves subjective sleep quality, insomnia severity and daytime sleepiness. Noted limitation from the review itself: the improvements are in subjective rather than physiological sleep measures.

claim_text: cancer loves sugar ... a cancer cell consumes 15 times the glucose of any other cell
notes: Elevated glucose uptake by tumour cells (the Warburg effect) is real and well described in the retrieved reviews, but the specific figure of 15 times any other cell is not supported by anything retrieved, and the reviews describe aerobic glycolysis as a requirement of proliferation rather than a feeding relationship with dietary sugar.

claim_text: Cancer also loves an acid environment
notes: Supported as stated, and deliberately labelled that way: 'The Acidic Tumor Microenvironment as a Driver of Cancer' is exactly this claim. The acidity is produced by the tumour's own metabolism inside the tumour, not set by what the person eats -- which is the step the next two claims take without support. A reviewer should read this row together with them.

claim_text: what is the most acid substance you can put into your body? Refined sugar ... when they extract the sugar out of the sugarcane plant it becomes a pure acid
notes: Dietary acid load is determined by protein, potassium, phosphorus, calcium and magnesium, plus organic acids that are metabolised to bicarbonate and so alkalinise. Refined sucrose contributes none of those, so it cannot be the most acidifying thing a person can eat. Medium confidence because the review defines the measure rather than naming sugar; a reviewer should check the PRAL framing in section 'What is acid-base status?' of PMC11006742.

claim_text: Cancer is not happy when you create an alkaline environment in the ... body
notes: Contradicted on the premise and unsupported on the outcome. Human acid-base equilibrium is, in the retrieved review's words, 'a tightly regulated physiological system that aims to maintain blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45', managed by the kidneys and lungs, so a diet cannot make the body alkaline. The systematic review of dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer located no studies at all examining alkaline diet or alkaline water for cancer treatment, and the single included cohort found no association. This is the claim that makes the video MISINFO.

claim_text: Cancer hates it when you stop the sugar or stop all glucose
notes: Glucose restriction as cancer therapy is still at the stage of proposing a clinical research framework (the retrieved paper is a framework proposal for ketogenic metabolic therapy in glioblastoma), so nothing yet tests the claim in patients. Not false, not established -- and dangerous as advice at 'no matter what stage', which is a materiality point for the reviewer rather than a verdict.

claim_text: remember genetics loads the gun, lifestyle pulls the trigger
notes: An aphorism, not a testable proposition. Kept as a row because it is doing argumentative work in the video, and NOT_VERIFIABLE is the honest verdict for it.

claim_text: Some do IV vitamin C, some do apricot kernel seeds [among doctors, specialists and naturopaths who are conquering cancer]
notes: A QUOTES row: the speaker reports what the authors of books in his library do, without asserting it himself in this sentence. Intravenous vitamin C has reached randomised phase 3 trials in combination chemotherapy, so it is being studied rather than established; a search for amygdalin, laetrile or apricot kernels against cancer returned nothing at all.

claim_text: All diabetics must avoid eating these four fruits
notes: Contradicted head-on. The meta-analysis of nineteen randomised controlled trials (888 participants) finds fruit consumption significantly lowers fasting blood glucose and concludes: 'we recommend that patients with diabetes eat more fruits while ensuring that their total energy intake remains unchanged'. The claim is the opposite of the evidence-based advice, and it is the claim that makes this video MISINFO under section 9.

claim_text: Watermelon has a very high glycemic index ... That means it raises blood sugar quickly, even in small portions
notes: Deliberately not lumped in with the apple and banana rows. Watermelon is the one fruit here with a genuinely high glycemic index, and the tables are not open access so no specific value could be read. The 'even in small portions' half is also questionable, since glycemic load accounts for portion and watermelon's is low -- but nothing retrieved states that, so it stays insufficient.

claim_text: Ripe bananas have a high glycemic index and sugar content, which can rapidly elevate blood sugar levels
notes: The 2021 international tables of glycemic index and glycemic load report that fruits are usually low-GI foods, at or below 55 on the 100-point glucose scale, with consistent values worldwide. Medium rather than high confidence because the tables are not open access, so this rests on the review's summary statement about fruits as a class rather than on the banana row itself.

claim_text: Mangos, especially when ripe, contain a lot of sugar that can cause quick blood sugar spikes
notes: No mango-specific value or trial was retrieved. The claim is also softer than the others ('can cause'), and it is paired with sensible portion advice.

claim_text: Apple has a high glycemic index and can sharply raise blood glucose
notes: Apples are a standard example of a low-GI fruit, and the 2021 international tables report fruits as usually low-GI (at or below 55). Same limitation as the banana row: the summary statement about fruits as a class is readable, the per-food table is not.

claim_text: Venus fly trap[s] ... you blend up three to four of them and eat[] them every day ... And that kills your cancer
notes: A search for Dionaea muscipula or Venus flytrap extract against cancer returned nothing at all; the empty search is in evidence_cache/. Section 7 is explicit that this is insufficient evidence and not CONTRADICTED, however implausible the claim sounds. The verdict is the easy part here; the stance is the judgement call.

claim_text: Over the last five years and typically healthy 30 to 40-year-olds, prostate cancer is up a whopping 500 percent
notes: The speaker's correction is about the time window, not the biology: she says the figure comes from 25 years of data (2000-2024), not five. Settling that needs the Australian cancer registry rather than a paper, and nothing retrieved tests it. The closest retrievable item is a report on rising early-onset cancer in Australia described explicitly 'over two decades', which is consistent with her correction but does not verify the 500% figure. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not yet checked. AIHW, Australia's national health statistics agency, is on the allow-list, but its cancer incidence data are interactive workbooks with no stable age-specific passage to quote; a reviewer with the AIHW 'Cancer data in Australia' workbook can settle the five-versus-25-year question.

claim_text: Scientists from around the world who are actually studying these trends point to things like improved screening, obesity trends, infections, and environmental exposures
notes: The early-onset cancer literature does attribute rising incidence to screening changes, metabolic and obesity trends and environmental exposures. Medium confidence because the retrieved reviews are concentrated on gastrointestinal and colorectal cancers rather than prostate cancer.

claim_text: when evidence showed that trans fat increased heart disease risk, independent scientists globally said it
notes: The systematic review and meta-analysis of industrial and ruminant trans fatty acids and coronary heart disease supports the premise of the analogy.

claim_text: If vaccines were causing increased cancer rates, independent researchers worldwide would say so
notes: A claim about how science behaves, not about health. No study could test it as stated, so NOT_VERIFIABLE. Kept as a row because it is the load-bearing argument of the video.

claim_text: Tea tree reduces all acne by 512 percent
notes: Tea tree oil does have a measured effect on acne, and that is what contradicts the claim: the comparative trial against benzoyl peroxide reports a modest effect with slower onset, nothing like a 512% reduction -- a figure that cannot describe a reduction at all, as the speaker points out himself.

claim_text: Macker [maca] root. Three times your pencil size in 30 days
notes: Nothing retrieved tests maca root against genital size. Refuted by incredulity rather than by evidence, which is a stance-detection case as much as a verdict one.

claim_text: Beat root [beetroot] spikes muscle growth in 30 days
notes: Refuted with a joke about Ronnie Coleman. Nothing retrieved tests beetroot against muscle growth over 30 days.

claim_text: Batana oil adds three inches of hair to your scalp ... Reverses you're balding completely
notes: Nothing retrieved tests batana oil for hair growth or androgenetic alopecia.

claim_text: It [tea tree] can actually be quite damaging to your skin if you apply it directly and don't dilute it down
notes: The speaker's own positive claim. The systematic review of essential oils as topical anti-infectives was retrieved but nothing readable in it addresses undiluted tea tree oil causing skin damage.

claim_text: If you go to get off of it, you gain all the weight back
notes: Stance UNCLEAR because this is the influencer's claim and the doctor never addresses it, so the video takes no position. The verdict is the interesting part: her claim is the best-supported one in the exchange. The STEP 1 trial extension found weight regain after semaglutide withdrawal, and a 2025 meta-analysis documents metabolic rebound after discontinuation. 'All the weight' overstates it -- STEP 1 participants regained about two thirds -- hence medium confidence.

claim_text: Ozympic [Ozempic] kills hunger. And that's one of the reasons it's causing people to lose weight
notes: The one claim both speakers accept, so ENDORSES is safe. Directly supported: the trial of once-weekly semaglutide measured effects on appetite, energy intake and control of eating.

claim_text: We don't know what it does to the microbiome ... If we destroy our microbiome, you destroy your body and you destroy your mind
notes: Refuted by the doctor and contradicted by the evidence: a systematic review of thirty-eight studies describes GLP-1 analogues' effects on gut microbiota composition, richness and diversity, with liraglutide promoting beneficial genera. 'We don't know' is no longer true. Medium confidence because much of that review is animal work.

claim_text: a fasting lifestyle will give you the same weight loss result and save you money as ozempic
notes: The SELECT long-term analysis and the STEP UP phase 3b trial put semaglutide weight loss well above what fasting achieves, which contradicts equivalence. A search for intermittent-fasting weight-loss magnitude returned nothing, so the fasting side of the comparison rests on the absence of comparable results rather than on a retrieved number.

claim_text: we should look at hard outcomes meaning improved cardiovascular health. We reduce risk of heart attacks
notes: The doctor's own claim, supported by the SELECT cardiovascular and kidney outcome analyses.

claim_text: You get less than a 10% total body weight loss with any type of fasting ... Whereas these medicines we're looking at 15 to 20 or higher percent total body weight loss
notes: The drug half of the comparison is well supported. The 'less than 10% with any type of fasting' half is not backed by anything retrieved, so a reviewer could reasonably split this row in two and mark the fasting half insufficient.

claim_text: Your body has a natural circadian rhythm that makes hunger hit its lowest point around 8AM
notes: Supported in direction by the circadian substrate-oxidation and ghrelin literature. The specific clock time of 8 a.m. is more precise than the retrieved studies state, which is why this is medium rather than high confidence.

claim_text: Growl in [ghrelin], your hunger hormone is naturally suppressed in the morning hours
notes: Directly supported: ghrelin is shown to be governed by the endogenous circadian system in humans. Note the transcript renders 'ghrelin' as 'growl in' -- a transcription artefact worth keeping for the extraction track, since a claim extractor reading the raw transcript loses the hormone's name.

claim_text: hunger and appetite peak later in the evening
notes: Consistent with the chrononutrition literature on diurnal appetite variation.

claim_text: poor sleep messes with your hunger hormones completely
notes: The retrieved paper covers circadian misalignment rather than sleep deprivation as such, and 'completely' is not a testable magnitude.

claim_text: the first word of advice I would give is to cut out any form of processed sugar. Starving cancer to death by removing one food in particular, refined sugars, could end up saving your life
notes: The retrieved work is a proposed clinical research framework for ketogenic metabolic therapy in glioblastoma and a review of diet in cancer development and management -- that is, the question is open and being formalised, not answered. Nothing tests whether removing refined sugar starves a tumour or extends survival. Flagged for review on materiality rather than on verdict.

claim_text: Japanese doctors during World War 2 accidentally discovered that miso soup was a preventative and a way to stop radiation exposure and radiation poisoning
notes: A historical claim about a wartime discovery. Nothing retrieved documents it; the firsthand accounts the speaker appeals to are not in the biomedical literature.

claim_text: they discovered that miso soup carried binders that would actually remove any form of radiation from the human body or the bloodstream
notes: There is a real radioprotection study -- 'Radioprotective effects of miso (fermented soy bean paste) against radiation in B6C3F1 mice' -- but it is in mice, and it reports radioprotection rather than binders removing radiation from the bloodstream. Fails directness twice over: wrong species and wrong mechanism.

claim_text: it demonstrated the potential for miso to prevent radiation poisoning ... So why not have a bowl of miso soup before getting any kind of X-rays?
notes: The claim is hedged to 'potential', which the mouse study arguably supports, but the recommendation it carries -- miso before diagnostic X-rays -- is not tested by anything retrieved.

claim_text: our entire physical makeup is comprised of 102 of these minerals in trace amounts
notes: Nothing retrieved states an element count for the human body. A reviewer with a biochemistry reference should expect to correct the figure.

claim_text: according to two-time Nobel Prize winning chemist Dr. Linus Pauling, you can trace every sickness, every disease and every ailment to a mineral deficiency. I happen to agree with them
notes: Recorded as ENDORSES, not QUOTES: he attributes it to Pauling and then says he agrees, which is adopting the claim. Nothing retrieved tests it or documents the attribution. THE ROW WHERE THE RUBRIC IS MOST VISIBLY TOO CAUTIOUS -- a sweeping claim refuted by the whole of infectious and genetic medicine still lands on insufficient because no paper bothers to say so.

claim_text: Burdock root contains all 102 of those minerals
notes: No composition analysis of burdock root was retrieved.

claim_text: Iris Seamos [Irish moss] is a gelatinous sea algae that contains 92 of those 102 minerals, and it's actually in concentrated amounts
notes: No composition analysis retrieved.

claim_text: moranga [moringa] powder ... has just about the highest concentration of vitamins of any plant on the earth
notes: Moringa leaf composition studies were retrieved and they do profile vitamins and minerals, but none ranks moringa against all other plants, which is what the superlative claims.

claim_text: there's an ingredients in the drug ozembic [Ozempic] called berberine
notes: Flatly false and the claim that makes this video MISINFO. Semaglutide is an acylated GLP-1 analogue, a peptide, as the discovery paper sets out; berberine is a plant alkaloid and is not a component of it. The video's entire argument rests on this.

claim_text: berberine is actually nature's metformin
notes: Berberine does improve glycaemic measures in randomised trials, which is the supporting side. The comparative analysis of oral insulin sensitizers places metformin and berberine differently, so equating them is not supported. MIXED rather than CONTRADICTED because the glucose-lowering half is real.

claim_text: the benefits of berberine, barberry are so astounding that even doctors are getting off the drug [metformin]
notes: An unquantified claim about what unnamed doctors do. No study could test it as stated.

claim_text: berberine is amazing because it has a multitude of health benefits, one of which is it helps to eliminate arterial plaque
notes: A search for berberine against atherosclerosis or arterial plaque regression returned nothing at all; the empty search is in evidence_cache/.

claim_text: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) updated the warning labels on Pfizer and Moderna's COVID-19 mRNA vaccines to include new information regarding the risks of myocarditis and pericarditis
notes: A regulatory action, settled from the FDA's own announcement now that section 6 allows it: 'The warning on myocarditis and pericarditis in the Prescribing Information for Comirnaty and Spikevax has been updated' (Comirnaty is Pfizer's and Spikevax Moderna's mRNA vaccine). Was INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE only because the old rules allowed literature alone.

claim_text: the risks of myocarditis and pericarditis, particularly in young males
notes: The health claim inside the news card, and it is well supported: the self-controlled case-series study of myocarditis, pericarditis and arrhythmia risks after COVID-19 vaccination or SARS-CoV-2 infection, the case series on myocarditis with mRNA vaccines, and the US adverse-event surveillance report. The young-male predominance is a consistent finding. Worth recording that an accurate vaccine safety-signal claim sits in the same dataset as the false vaccine claims in v78 and v18 -- a classifier that treats 'vaccine' plus 'heart risk' as a misinformation signal will fail here.

claim_text: seed oils are unhealthy, leads to inflammation, heart disease, obesity
notes: Same myth and same contradicting evidence as v19: dietary linoleic acid is inversely associated with coronary heart disease risk in a dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts.

claim_text: that carbs make you fat
notes: Searches for isocaloric low-carbohydrate against low-fat comparisons returned trials in specific clinical populations rather than a test of the general claim, so nothing retrieved settles it.

claim_text: butter should be eaten as a snack and it is healthy for you to do so
notes: The same saturated-fat split as v11: Cochrane finds benefit from reducing saturated fat, a 2025 meta-analysis finds none. The evidence does not settle whether eating butter as a snack is healthy, so the refutation lands on MIXED.

claim_text: You can gain fat in a calorie deficit due to hormonal problems or endocrine dysfunction
notes: Nothing retrieved tests this. The speaker's counter-argument is from first principles ('you are still bound to the laws of physics') rather than from a study, which is a reasonable argument and still not retrievable evidence.

claim_text: that vegetables are bad for you
notes: Contradicted by the systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of fruit and vegetable intake against cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality, and by the two-cohort mortality analysis.

claim_text: Electrolytes help you properly retain fluid, keeping you way more hydrated
notes: The Beverage Hydration Index work shows electrolyte content influences fluid retention, and the sodium rehydration trial supports the mechanism. Both are in exercise-rehydration settings rather than healthy people adding electrolytes to morning water, which is a directness limitation.

claim_text: So think better, energy levels, immune health, and no more headaches
notes: Three separate outcomes asserted in one breath with no mechanism and no magnitude. Nothing retrieved tests electrolyte supplementation against energy, immune function or headaches in this population. Kept as one row because it is one list in one clause, not three developed claims.

claim_text: Scrub your entire hands up to just above your wrists for 20 seconds
notes: The quantification study reports a 1.7 log CFU reduction for a 20-second wash with soap against 1.0 log for a 5-second wash without, so the 20-second duration with soap is the better-supported procedure. Medium confidence because the same paper finds some comparisons not statistically significant.

claim_text: Use a piece of paper towel to turn off the faucet
notes: An instruction from public-health handwashing guidance, so a fact of record: the NHS method's step 11 is 'Use the disposable towel to turn off the tap.' Previously INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE because no study tests the step; the claim is that this is the guidance, and the guidance says so. Whether the step reduces recontamination remains untested, and that is a different (research) claim.

claim_text: What are the most harmful foods that people constantly eat? Seed oils
notes: The dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts finds dietary linoleic acid inversely associated with coronary heart disease risk, which contradicts seed oils being the most harmful food people eat.

claim_text: you de-gum it with hexane, which is a known neurotoxin
notes: Deliberately labelled SUPPORTED. n-hexane really is a neurotoxin -- occupational exposure causes peripheral neuropathy, as the toxicity review and the automotive-technician cluster report show. The claim as stated is true; the inference the video draws from it, that refined seed oil is therefore harmful to eat, is a separate claim and is the one the evidence contradicts. A reviewer should read this row next to the inflammation row -- this is how true fragments carry a false conclusion.

claim_text: You need to deodorize it with sodium hydroxide, which is a very powerful carcinogen
notes: A search for sodium hydroxide toxicity and carcinogenicity returned nothing at all; the empty search is in evidence_cache/. Sodium hydroxide is handled as a corrosive rather than a carcinogen, but no retrieved source says so, so this stays insufficient rather than contradicted. Another row a reviewer with a toxicology reference should expect to upgrade. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): no allow-listed reference was retrieved. Note that an agency's 'not classified as a carcinogen' would itself be absence of a finding, which section 6 says keeps the claim INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE rather than CONTRADICTED.

claim_text: These are pro-inflammatory that cause massive amount of inflammation in the body
notes: The claim that makes this video MISINFO, and the best-evidenced contradiction in the bundle. The systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials found no significant effect of higher linoleic acid intake on tumour necrosis factor, interleukin-6, adiponectin or monocyte chemoattractant protein 1, and a second systematic review of randomised trials in healthy people agrees.

claim_text: in your kitchen, you need five oils. You need a grass-fed butter, butter, grass-fed tallow, coconut oil, and an olive oil
notes: A recommendation rather than a mechanism claim, and nothing retrieved tests this specific set of five fats. Cited against is the Cochrane review on reducing saturated fat, since four of the five recommended fats are saturated-fat-dominant, but that bears on the recommendation rather than testing it.

notes: An unidentified individual, no date, no location, no cause of death, and the video itself switches the subject's gender mid-story ('what happened to him'). There is no version of this a study could test.

notes: A search for ancient microorganisms in glacial ice and permafrost and their viability returned nothing at all; the empty search is in evidence_cache/. The claim also contains a false premise about glacier ages that is geological rather than medical and so is not a row here.

claim_text: You get the injection in your arm ... Most often little pieces of the pathogen

notes: The pre-existing randomly generated repertoire is standard immunology and the retrieved papers are consistent with it, but neither tests this claim head-on, so medium confidence.

notes: The equivalence between infection-induced and vaccine-induced priming, which is the video's central point.

notes: The best NEUTRAL example in the set. The scientist says in terms 'I don't know of data to say one way or the other', so he discusses the claim without taking a position -- section 5's NEUTRAL, not UNCLEAR, because there is nothing ambiguous about his meaning. notes: The systematic review of marijuana smoking and the respiratory system supports both halves, including the specific point that cannabis smoke is not benign for the lungs. notes: The cohort of veterans with coronary artery disease supports an association between cannabis smoking and cardiovascular events. Medium confidence because nothing retrieved pins the effect size to the 1.3-2x range he quotes.

notes: A comparative magnitude claim across three risk factors. Nothing retrieved puts them on the same scale, so the comparison is untested.

notes: Clinical anecdote from his own operating theatre. Not the kind of claim a study tests, and recorded as NOT_VERIFIABLE rather than dismissed, since unverifiable testimony from a credible speaker is exactly what makes health content persuasive.

claim_text: 10 minutes after your meal, glucose starts flooding your bloodstream. If you sit down, that sugar just sits there forcing your body to pump out excess insulin
notes: Breaking up prolonged sitting does reduce postprandial glucose and insulin responses, which is the claim's substance. The 'ten minutes' timing is more precise than the trials specify.

notes: Brief bouts of light walking or simple resistance activity improve glucose handling in type 2 diabetes, which supports the mechanism. The specific prescription of 15 chair squats is not itself tested.

notes: The retrieved review of consumer antibacterial soaps supports the claim and also the speaker's follow-up about antibiotic resistance concerns driving US regulatory changes.

claim_text: This idea of just drink more water to have nice skin, total BS. Drinking excessive amounts of water will not make your skin look different
notes: Nothing retrieved tests water intake against skin appearance in people with normal fluid balance. Note that he qualifies the claim carefully himself ('assuming normal fluid balance'), which per section 4 has to be preserved in the claim text.

claim_text: we don't know like what the optimal amount of water a standard adult human should be drinking every day is ... three liters or eight eight ounce glasses or what like that's not evidence-based
notes: A claim ABOUT the absence of evidence. Retrieving nothing is consistent with him being right, but section 7's INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE means 'we cannot say', so the verdict cannot express agreement with a negative claim. Independently, this is the third video in the set (with v07 and v12) to turn on the same hydration-rule evidence gap, from a third direction.

notes: Consistent with the retrieved review of over-the-counter acne treatment, which treats acne as an inflammatory condition rather than an infection.

notes: A search for nut consumption against all-cause mortality and life expectancy returned nothing, and the specific Michigan analysis was not retrieved. Checkable in principle -- it is a named study -- which makes this a retrieval failure rather than an evidence gap, and a good test case for the retrieval track.

claim_text: they have so many amazing things for your health, but because they're high calorie, people think they're unhealthy
notes: The retrieved review of nuts, energy balance and body weight is adjacent but does not test an unquantified 'so many amazing things'.

claim_text: low calorie and healthy aren't the same thing
notes: A definitional point rather than an empirical claim.

notes: An analogy standing in for immunological memory, which the retrieved review covers. Supported in substance; the analogy itself is not what a study tests.

notes: A correct description of innate immunity and fever as a host response.

notes: A search for the asymptomatic and paralytic proportions of poliomyelitis infection returned nothing; the empty search is in evidence_cache/. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled. WHO's polio fact sheet gives only 'One in 200 infections leads to irreversible paralysis', and the StatPearls chapter abstract (PMID 32644370) says only that 'most infections are asymptomatic'; neither tests 90%. CDC's Pink Book chapter, which gives a percentage, refuses scripted retrieval (HTTP 403).

notes: Supported in substance by the systematic review of smoking against lung cancer, COPD, ischaemic heart disease and stroke, and by the Mendelian randomisation analysis across 24 gastrointestinal diseases. The superlative ('one single thing ... as much damage') is a ranking nothing retrieved tests, hence medium.

notes: The meta-analysis of cigarette smoking across major histological types of lung cancer. As directly supported as a claim in this set gets.

notes: Measles' extreme transmissibility is well established and the retrieved airborne-transmission modelling study is consistent with it, but a superlative across all known viruses is a ranking claim that nothing retrieved tests. WHO's measles fact sheet calls measles 'one of the world's most contagious diseases', which supports high transmissibility but not the superlative.

notes: The Cochrane review of measles, mumps, rubella and varicella vaccines in children was retrieved and supports vaccine effectiveness, but nothing retrieved tests infant measles mortality or the cocooning mechanism specifically.

notes: Nothing tests this preparation, and the five-minute onset is implausible on any mechanism. notes: A superlative ranking muscle mass above all other protective factors, including screening and not smoking. Nothing retrieved supports that ranking, though the sarcopenia literature supports the weaker claim underneath it.

notes: The skin-absorption study reports an absorbed dose after 24 hours of exposure of 25% for BPA and 17% for one alternative, with the handling study addressing dermal exposure from thermal paper directly. This is the row that makes the collectors' MISINFO label look wrong.

notes: Follows from the handling study's exposure implications. Note what the video does not claim: no disease outcome is asserted, which is why nothing here is overreach.

notes: Pharmaceutical residues in water bodies are real and measured. What the video omits, and the retrieved risk assessments address, is that detection at trace concentrations is not the same as a health risk. Supported as literally stated.

claim_text: [the CDC] updated their site to say that vaccines may cause autism
notes: The health claim inside the reported agency change, which he refutes. Contradicted by the evidence-based meta-analysis titled 'Vaccines are not associated with autism', the Cochrane review, and the thimerosal medical-records study.

notes: His own positive claim, supported by the meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies and the Cochrane review. notes: Supported by the physical-activity and cardiovascular mortality review and the resistance-training meta-analysis. The fracture limb is the least directly evidenced of the three.

notes: The sleep half is directly supported by the same meta-analyses used for v26. The anxiety and depression half is supported in direction but nothing retrieved here tests it specifically.

notes: The systematic review of physical activity and cognitive decline and the midlife modifiable risk-factor meta-analysis support the dementia limb. Self-esteem is untested here.

notes: The review of physical activity, obesity and sedentary behaviour in cancer aetiology supports the multi-site association, and the brisk-walking review supports the blood-pressure limb. Kept as one row rather than eight: the speaker asserts one association across sites, and splitting per site would invent eight claims he did not separately make.

notes: Directly supported by the physical activity and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality review and the daily step-count analysis.

notes: A claim about what guidelines say, settled by the guideline itself now that section 6 allows it: WHO says adults aged 18-64 'should do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity throughout the week, or do at least 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity'.

notes: The claim the whole video exists to refute, and it cannot be adjudicated here. Settling it needs the AAP, CDC and European national schedules, none of which is a paper. Under section 9 that leaves a thorough, numerate debunk labelled CANNOT_RECOGNIZE. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled. CDC's schedule pages refuse scripted retrieval (HTTP 403), and no other allow-listed source carries the US and European schedules as countable documents. Under the revised section 9 the video is still CANNOT_RECOGNIZE, but it now goes to review as a possible debunk of an unsettled claim.

notes: His own count from the AAP schedule. Same problem: a schedule document, not a study. Section 6 reference search (2026-11-22): not settled; CDC's schedule pages refuse scripted retrieval (HTTP 403).
